Process

How a project actually runs.

Eight stages, and the part most process pages leave out is here: what we need from you at each one. That is not a formality. Whether a project works is decided almost entirely by whether one named person on your side has the time, and it is better to find that out in week one than in week nine.

A standard scope for a business of 10 to 100 people runs in weeks, not quarters. Heavy migration, bespoke work or a phased rollout across several teams pushes it toward a quarter, staged. Any timeline is on the written scope with the price, not left to be discovered.

The eight stages

In the order they happen, with what each one costs you in attention.

  1. 1. The first conversation

    Thirty to forty-five minutes, mostly us asking how work actually moves through your business. Not slides. The useful output is often that we are wrong for you — no point of sale, no manufacturing planning, no multi-entity consolidation — and twenty minutes is usually enough to establish it. From you: someone who knows how the work really happens, which is frequently not the owner. The owner knows what the process is supposed to be.

  2. 2. The written scope and a fixed number

    Usually within one business day. Modules, users, what we migrate, what we build, the timeline, the price, and a named list of what we are not doing. It is yours to keep and circulate whether or not you proceed. From you: one person to read the exclusions properly and argue with them. Almost every project that goes wrong went wrong here, in a line somebody skimmed.

  3. 3. Data assessment, before you sign

    Send the spreadsheets and a Tally export and we will tell you what imports cleanly and what does not, in writing, before money changes hands. What we typically find: four spellings of the same company, phone numbers in six formats, missing or invalid GSTINs, opening balances nobody can tie to a trial balance. From you: a decision about who is the authority when two records conflict. That is a business judgement and we cannot make it for you.

  4. 4. Build and configuration

    Your fields, your pipeline stages, your document templates, your approval rules, your ledger and cost-centre mapping for the Tally export. Your GST registrations, your HSN and SAC codes, your TDS sections by vendor type, your MSME vendor list. From you: the actual documents — a real invoice, a real quote, a real demand letter — rather than a description of them. A template built from a description is wrong in exactly the places somebody will notice in front of a customer.

  5. 5. Migration, dry run first

    History goes into a separate workspace and is reconciled before anything is live. Reconciled against a number you already trust and can defend — the trial balance, the total receivables outstanding, the closing stock value. Nothing goes live on a migration nobody has checked. From you: the person who can say the receivables total should be two point one crore and be right. If nobody in the business can state that number, that is the finding, and it matters more than the migration.

  6. 6. Pilot with one team

    One team, one module, two to four weeks. Not a department-wide launch and not a training session followed by hope. The pilot exists to find the three things about your business that no scoping conversation surfaces. From you: permission for that team to stop doing it the old way. Running both systems in parallel feels safe and is the most reliable way to kill a rollout — people revert to what they know at the first busy week, and the new system quietly becomes double entry.

  7. 7. Rollout, module by module

    In the order that money hurts, not the order that is tidy. Training is short and shaped by role: a salesperson gets forty minutes on their own morning list, not a two-hour tour of the whole product. A person only needs to learn the screen they will open at nine. From you: managers who use it themselves. A manager who asks for the numbers by WhatsApp has told their team the system is optional, and no amount of training beats that signal.

  8. 8. The first ninety days

    Weekly for the first month, then fortnightly. We look at four things: is anyone logging in daily, is any queue growing rather than clearing, has month-end got shorter, and what are people still doing in a spreadsheet. That last one is the most useful question in the whole process. From you: honesty in those calls. A team that says it is going fine for six weeks and then stops using it costs everyone a quarter.

What we need from you, in one list

Consolidated so you can decide up front whether you have this. If you do not, say so and we will scope smaller rather than plan around capacity that does not exist.

  • One named owner and one deputy, with real time — a few hours a week during the build, more during the pilot. Not a name on a slide.
  • Decisions when we ask for them. The single biggest cause of a slipped date is a question that sat unanswered for nine days, and the second is a decision made and then reversed.
  • Real documents, real data, real edge cases. Send us the invoice that always breaks the template, not the clean one.
  • Someone who can say what a key number should be and defend it.
  • Permission for the pilot team to stop the old way, from someone senior enough that it holds when it gets busy.

What we handle, so nobody is waiting on you for it

Everything here is inside the quoted price unless the scope names it as excluded.

  • Hosting, backups, security updates and every platform improvement we ship.
  • Configuration — fields, stages, templates, rules, mappings. You describe it, we build it.
  • The migration itself: cleaning, mapping, loading, and reconciling to your numbers.
  • Training, remote, by role. On-site is quoted separately and most teams do not need it.
  • Support from the people who wrote the code, with no first-tier queue in front of them.

What goes wrong, and what we do about it

Three failure modes account for nearly all of it. None of them are surprises and all of them are survivable if named early.

  • Dirty data. Eleven years of records with four spellings of one company and no consistent phone format. We deduplicate on phone number and flag the rest, but we cannot decide which of four Sharma Traders is the real customer — that needs somebody who was there. A clean system loaded with dirty data is a more expensive spreadsheet, so we would rather delay a go-live by a week than launch on records nobody believes.
  • Adoption. The people who lived in the old spreadsheet are the slowest to move, which is normal — it was their spreadsheet and they were good at it. Training does not fix this and neither does a mandate. What fixes it is the morning list being genuinely faster than opening four tabs. If it is not faster by week six, the design is wrong, and we cut features rather than run another session.
  • Scope creep. Small changes are part of the subscription and we do not bill for them, because nickel-and-diming a field change poisons the relationship. Anything larger gets a written change note with a price before we build it. We do not build first and invoice after, and we do not silently absorb work and then get slow.
  • The fourth one, which nobody lists: a module scoped, built and then ignored. On one project a production-scheduling piece looked essential on paper and turned out to be a problem the warehouse had already solved with a whiteboard. Better to drop it at the pilot than to have paid for it.

What we will not do

No big-bang launch across every department on one Monday. We have been asked for it and we have said no, because it removes the only mechanism that catches a wrong assumption cheaply.

No six-month discovery phase before anything exists. If you are paying for months of workshops, you are paying for somebody to postpone being wrong. Our scoping is a conversation and a document, and the price is on the document.

No consultants billing by the day on your site indefinitely. On-site training is a line item with a number, not an open meter. And we will not put four people on a project to look substantial — you will deal with the person who built the thing you are asking about.

Questions people actually ask

How much of our time does this really take?

For a standard scope: a few hours a week from one person during the build, more like a day a week from the pilot team for two to four weeks, then an hour every week or two for the first ninety days. If that sounds like more than you have, the answer is a smaller first module, not a heroic plan.

Can you just do it without involving our team?

No, and any vendor who says yes is selling you a system that will be abandoned. We can build a configuration from documents alone. We cannot make your team open it on a Monday, and that is what you are actually buying.

What if we need to stop halfway?

You can stop after the conversation, after the scope, or after the data assessment, and none of those cost you anything. Once building has started, the commercial terms apply and they are on the site. What we will not do is keep building something we can both see is not working.

Start at stage one.

Thirty minutes, mostly questions, and an honest answer about whether this is worth either of our time. Nobody is put through a qualification script.
